latest_nl_proof:
Fix integers m,g with m\ge 2 and g\ge 0.

We will construct mutually inverse maps between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}.

First, for S\in A_{m,g}, define for each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}
\[
w_i:=\min\{s\in S: s\equiv i\pmod m\}.
\]
This is well-defined: since \mathbb N_0\setminus S is finite, there exists M such that every integer n\ge M lies in S. For any fixed residue class i mod m, there are arbitrarily large integers congruent to i mod m, so some such integer lies in S; hence the displayed set is nonempty. As it is a nonempty subset of \mathbb N_0, it has a least element.

Because the least positive element of S is m, none of 1,2,\dots,m-1 belongs to S. Therefore w_i cannot equal i, so w_i>i. Since w_i\equiv i\pmod m}, there is a unique integer k_i\ge 1 such that
\[
w_i=k_i m+i.
\]
Thus we obtain a tuple
\[
\Phi(S):=(k_1,\dots,k_{m-1}).
\]
We show that \Phi(S)\in K_{m,g}.

1. Positivity of coordinates has already been shown: each k_i\in \mathbb Z_{>0}.

2. Kunz inequalities. Let 1\le i\le j\le m-1.

If i+j<m, then w_i+w_j\in S by closure of S under addition, and
\[
w_i+w_j\equiv i+j\pmod m.
\]
By minimality of w_{i+j} among elements of S congruent to i+j mod m, we have
\[
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j}.
\]
Substituting w_t=k_t m+t gives
\[
(k_i m+i)+(k_j m+j)\ge k_{i+j}m+(i+j),
\]
hence
\[
k_i+k_j\ge k_{i+j}.
\]

If i+j>m, then w_i+w_j\in S and
\[
w_i+w_j\equiv i+j-m\pmod m.
\]
By minimality of w_{i+j-m},
\[
w_i+w_j\ge w_{i+j-m}.
\]
Substituting gives
\[
(k_i m+i)+(k_j m+j)\ge k_{i+j-m}m+(i+j-m),
\]
so
\[
(k_i+k_j+1)m\ge k_{i+j-m}m,
\]
and therefore
\[
k_i+k_j+1\ge k_{i+j-m}.
\]
This is exactly the required inequality. (As in the definition, no condition is needed when i+j=m.)

3. Sum condition. We claim that
\[
|\mathbb N_0\setminus S|=k_1+\cdots+k_{m-1}.
\]
Indeed, for each residue i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the minimal element of S in that residue class is w_i=k_i m+i. Hence the numbers in that residue class that are not in S are exactly
\[
i,\; m+i,\; 2m+i,\; \dots,\; (k_i-1)m+i.
\]
There are exactly k_i such numbers. Also, among multiples of m, none is missing from S: 0\in S and m\in S, so by closure every multiple tm=(t-1)m+m belongs to S for all t\ge 1. Therefore the complement \mathbb N_0\setminus S is the disjoint union over i=1,\dots,m-1 of those k_i missing numbers in residue class i, and its cardinality is \sum_i k_i. Since S\in A_{m,g}, this cardinality equals g. Hence
\[
k_1+\cdots+k_{m-1}=g.
\]
So \Phi(S)\in K_{m,g}.

Thus \Phi:A_{m,g}\to K_{m,g} is well-defined.

Now define a map in the opposite direction. Let k=(k_1,\dots,k_{m-1})\in K_{m,g}. For each i=1,\dots,m-1, set
\[
w_i:=k_i m+i,
\]
and define
\[
\Psi(k):=\{0\}\cup \{qm:q\in\mathbb N, q\ge 1\}\cup \bigcup_{i=1}^{m-1}\{w_i+tm:t\in \mathbb N_0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \Psi(k) consists of 0, all positive multiples of m, and in each nonzero residue class i mod m, all integers congruent to i mod m that are at least w_i.

We show that \Psi(k)\in A_{m,g}.

1. 0\in \Psi(k) by definition.

2. \Psi(k) is closed under addition. Take a,b\in \Psi(k). We consider cases.

- If one of a,b is 0, then a+b is the other element, hence belongs to \Psi(k).

- If both are multiples of m, then a+b is a multiple of m, hence in \Psi(k).

- If a is a positive multiple of m and b=w_i+tm for some i and t\ge 0, then a+b=w_i+(t+q)m for some q\ge 1, so a+b\in \Psi(k). The same holds with a and b interchanged.

- If a=w_i+tm and b=w_j+um with 1\le i,j\le m-1 and t,u\ge 0, then
\[
a+b=w_i+w_j+(t+u)m.
\]
If i+j<m, the defining inequality of K_{m,g} gives k_i+k_j\ge k_{i+j}, hence
\[
w_i+w_j=(k_i+k_j)m+(i+j)\ge k_{i+j}m+(i+j)=w_{i+j}.
\]
Therefore a+b\ge w_{i+j} and a+b\equiv i+j\pmod m, so a+b belongs to the tail \{w_{i+j}+rm:r\in\mathbb N_0\}\subseteq \Psi(k).

If i+j=m, then
\[
w_i+w_j=(k_i+k_j+1)m,
\]
which is a positive multiple of m, so a+b\in \Psi(k).

If i+j>m, the defining inequality gives k_i+k_j+1\ge k_{i+j-m}, hence
\[
w_i+w_j=(k_i+k_j)m+(i+j)\ge k_{i+j-m}m+(i+j-m)=w_{i+j-m}.
\]
Also a+b\equiv i+j-m\pmod m, so again a+b lies in the corresponding tail and hence in \Psi(k).

All cases are covered, so \Psi(k) is closed under addition.

3. \mathbb N_0\setminus \Psi(k) is finite. Indeed, in residue class 0 mod m, every multiple of m belongs to \Psi(k). In residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, every number \ge w_i and congruent to i mod m belongs to \Psi(k), so the only missing numbers in that class are
\[
i,\; m+i,\; 2m+i,\; \dots,\; (k_i-1)m+i,
\]
which is a finite set. Since there are only finitely many residue classes, the complement is finite.

4. The least positive element of \Psi(k) is m. Since each k_i\ge 1, we have w_i=k_i m+i\ge m+i>m for every i=1,\dots,m-1. Thus no element of \Psi(k) in a nonzero residue class is less than or equal to m. On the other hand m itself is in \Psi(k) as a positive multiple of m. Therefore the least positive element is exactly m.

5. The genus equals g. As observed above, in residue class 0 mod m there are no missing numbers, and in residue class i the missing numbers are exactly
\[
i,\; m+i,\; \dots,\; (k_i-1)m+i,
\]
so there are exactly k_i of them. Hence
\[
|\mathbb N_0\setminus \Psi(k)|=k_1+\cdots+k_{m-1}=g,
\]
using the defining condition of K_{m,g}.

Therefore \Psi(k)\in A_{m,g}. So \Psi:K_{m,g}\to A_{m,g} is well-defined.

It remains to show that \Phi and \Psi are inverse bijections.

First let S\in A_{m,g}. Construct k=\Phi(S), so w_i=k_i m+i is the least element of S in residue class i. We claim that \Psi(k)=S. In residue class 0 mod m, both sets contain exactly all multiples of m: these are all in S because 0,m\in S and S is closed under addition, and they are all in \Psi(k) by definition. In residue class i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, by minimality of w_i, no smaller number congruent to i mod m lies in S; and if x\in S with x\equiv i\pmod m, then x\ge w_i, so x=w_i+tm for some t\ge 0. Conversely every w_i+tm lies in S because w_i,m\in S and S is closed under addition. Thus S and \Psi(k) have exactly the same elements in each residue class, hence are equal.

Second let k\in K_{m,g}. Form S=\Psi(k). For each i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}, the least element of S congruent to i mod m is exactly w_i=k_i m+i, because by construction every smaller number in that residue class is omitted from S. Therefore \Phi(S)=(k_1,\dots,k_{m-1})=k.

So \Phi and \Psi are inverse maps. Hence there exists a bijection between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}.

Consequently,
\[
N(m,g)=|A_{m,g}|=|K_{m,g}|.
\]
This is exactly the claimed statement.
role_in_parent: Transfers the original counting problem from numerical semigroups to Kunz-coordinate layers.
statement_nl: Fix integers m and g with m >= 2 and g >= 0. Define A_{m,g} to be the set of all subsets S of N0 = {0,1,2,...} such that: 0 belongs to S, S is closed under addition, N0 \ S is finite, the least positive element of S is m, and |N0 \ S| = g. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples k = (k_1, ..., k_{m-1}) of positive integers such that: for all integers i and j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}, and also k_1 + ... + k_{m-1} = g. Then there exists a bijection between A_{m,g} and K_{m,g}. Consequently, if N(m,g) denotes the cardinality |A_{m,g}|, then N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.

domain_restrictions: m is an integer with m ≥ 2.
g is an integer with g ≥ 0.
A_{m,g} only contains subsets S ⊆ N0.
In A_{m,g}: S is closed under addition, i.e., ∀ a,b ∈ S, a+b ∈ S.
In A_{m,g}: N0 \ S is finite (so |N0 \ S| is well-defined as a finite integer).
In A_{m,g}: the least positive element of S exists and equals m, i.e., m ∈ S and ∀ t ∈ N, 1 ≤ t < m implies t ∉ S.
K_{m,g} only contains tuples k = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) of positive integers, i.e., k_i ∈ Z_{>0} for each i ∈ {1,...,m-1}.
In K_{m,g}: inequalities are quantified over integers i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1.
For the case i+j < m: the index i+j lies in {2,...,m-1}, so k_{i+j} is among the tuple coordinates.
For the case i+j > m: the index i+j-m lies in {1,...,m-2}, so k_{i+j-m} is among the tuple coordinates.
No inequality is imposed when i+j = m (neither i+j < m nor i+j > m).
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all integers m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, the sets A_{m,g} and K_{m,g} are in bijection; hence with N(m,g) := |A_{m,g}|, one has N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.
quantifier_order: Fix (i.e., take arbitrary but fixed) m,g ∈ Z with m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0.
A_{m,g} is defined by: for all S ⊆ N0, S ∈ A_{m,g} iff (0 ∈ S) ∧ (∀ a,b ∈ S, a+b ∈ S) ∧ (N0 \ S is finite) ∧ (min(S\{0}) = m) ∧ (|N0 \ S| = g).

K_{m,g} is defined by: for all tuples k = (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) with k_i ∈ Z_{>0}, k ∈ K_{m,g} iff (∀ i,j ∈ Z, 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1: [if i+j < m then k_i+k_j ≥ k_{i+j}] ∧ [if i+j > m then k_i+k_j+1 ≥ k_{i+j-m}]) ∧ (∑_{t=1}^{m-1} k_t = g).
There exists a bijection f such that f: A_{m,g} → K_{m,g} is bijective (dependence allowed on m,g).

witness_dependencies: The bijection f exists for each fixed pair (m,g); i.e., f may depend on m and g.
Membership conditions for S ∈ A_{m,g} depend on m and g through: (i) least positive element equals m, and (ii) complement size equals g.
Membership conditions for k ∈ K_{m,g} depend on m and g through: (i) tuple length is m-1, (ii) the inequalities reference indices relative to m, and (iii) sum equals g.
